mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Saturday, August 15, 2026. Dutch officials have issued a warning regarding a high-severity vulnerability in macOS that is currently being exploited in the wild. The Netherlands National Cyber Security Centrum reported earlier this week that attackers are targeting systems where port 5900 is accessible from the internet. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-65400, affects the macOS screen sharing capability and allows unauthorized remote parties to view screens and control keyboards or mice. Investigators have observed attackers gaining root access—the highest level of administrative privilege—to deploy crypto miners on affected machines. Apple released a patch for the vulnerability last week for macOS Tahoe, Sequoia, and Sonoma. While Apple stated that the bug "may" allow access without credentials, security experts note that such language is typical in vulnerability disclosures. In Indonesia, the government, industry partners, and academia have launched the nation’s first university-based AI technology center. The UGM Indosat NVIDIA AI Technology Center was established at Universitas Gadjah Mada to help the country develop local AI talent and address national priorities. Supported by NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform and Indosat’s GPU-as-a-service infrastructure, the center aims to foster innovation in sectors like healthcare, agriculture, and disaster response. The initiative includes specific projects, such as the development of AI-powered electronic sensors to detect tuberculosis in rural areas. The move is part of a broader push to position Indonesia as a developer of AI technology rather than just a user. Google announced on Friday that it will allow users to toggle off visible watermarks on AI-generated images, videos, and music. This setting will be available in Gemini, the company’s video editor Flow, and eventually in Search for models including Nano Banana, Omni, and Lyria. The company clarified that this change does not impact invisible watermarks, such as SynthID, or metadata based on the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) standard. Google intends to balance creative flexibility with transparency, as invisible markers remain in place to help identify AI-generated content. Additionally, Google is open-sourcing a library called Credentio to help developers integrate local validation mechanisms into their own applications. In other infrastructure developments, Amazon Web Services detailed new ways to build agentic workflows, which are AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks. The company provided technical guidance on using Amazon Nova Forge to create custom reward functions for multi-turn reinforcement learning. This process allows developers to guide models through iterative feedback rather than static examples. Simultaneously, AWS outlined an architecture for integrating specialized models, such as the Qwen 3.5 9B, into Amazon Bedrock AgentCore workflows. These tools are designed to give developers more flexibility in mixing managed foundation models with cost-optimized, domain-specific models. In a separate matter, a PBS affiliate is currently involved in a legal dispute to recover 50 terabytes of archived data. Nine PBS in St. Louis sued Iron Mountain Data Centers after its former cloud storage provider, Open Source Storage, became unresponsive. The station’s archives, which contain 70 years of historical footage, were stored at an Iron Mountain facility. A judge recently ordered Iron Mountain to release the data to the station, provided that Nine PBS can facilitate the retrieval through a third party without compromising other client data. Finally, Meta released a new open-weight model called Glimmer this week, allowing users to run the technology on their own hardware. The release accompanied a manifesto from CEO Mark Zuckerberg advocating for broader access to AI tools. Industry analysts have noted that while the release promotes the idea of accessible AI, it contrasts with Meta’s more powerful models, which remain restricted behind proprietary APIs. Looking ahead, expect to see continued focus on the intersection of AI accessibility and safety as companies like Google and Meta navigate the balance between user control and the need for standardized identification of AI-generated media.
